newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: S.Africa plans to tackle land ownership this year.
newsitem.headline: S.Africa plans to tackle land ownership this year.

text.p: President Nelson Mandela's government will make a start this year on trying to resolve the tough and complex issue of South African land ownership, the land affairs minister Derek Hanekom said on Monday.
Three years after the first all-race elections some 80 percent of land is still owned by whites, who make up just 13 percent of the population.
Hanekom said the government would attempt this year to settle land disputes in the old nominally independent black homelands, which were recognised only by apartheid South Africa.
Hanekom said the process was complex because no title deeds existed for those territories -- comprising some 13 percent of the country's land.

"Our view is that essentially under a different history the people living on that land would have been, and ought to be, the owners and ought to have properly recognised rights," Hanekom told a news briefing.
Claims and counter-claims have been made by tribal authorities, existing communities and by elected local authorities keen to develop the land for agriculture, housing and commerce.
The lands minister said the government planned to draw up a comprehensive and detailed policy this year to prepare for legislation.

Hanekom said another key government focus this year would be implementation of the Extension of Security of Tenure Bill, which aims to stop unfair evictions, a fate that yearly befalls thousands of mainly black farmworkers and tenants living on white-owned land.

The bill, which will soon begin passage through parliament, has drawn sharp criticism from the white-dominated South African Agricultural Union which says it gives the government "extraordinary and unacceptable powers" to interfere in tenant-owner relations.
